docs.title: SharedHousehold Docs & Reports
docs.text:
The public site for SharedHousehold documentation, decisions, and agent reports.

  • Source of truth: the private repository share-org/share (docs/)
  • Site: this site is built with MkDocs Material and published automatically from the repository's docs/ directory.

docs.title: Latest reports
docs.text:
• BR-002 — Expense shares (EXP-105) decision Domain-first allocation engine with on-demand balances.
  • BR-001 — Agent permission architecture
  • ADR-001 — Agent permission restrictions

docs.title: Republishing
docs.text: The site republishes automatically when docs change on main. To force a republish, run the docs-publish workflow from the Actions tab of share-org/share (see docs/development/docs-publishing.md).

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
Human
  -> GitHub issue
  -> [brainstorming when a design decision exists]
  -> product-planner
  -> architect
  -> implementation agent (backend and/or frontend)
  -> qa-engineer
  -> code-reviewer
  -> security-reviewer (when relevant)
  -> Human review
  -> Merge

The orchestrator decides whether brainstorming is needed before planning. See docs/ai/brainstorms/ for decision reports and the brainstorming skill.

docs.title: Default workflow (minimum set required)
docs.text:
Issue
  -> [brainstorming when a design decision exists]
  -> product-planner
  -> architect
  -> implementation agent
  -> qa-engineer
  -> code-reviewer
  -> security-reviewer (when relevant)
  -> human review
  • Use documentation only when documentation actually changes.
  • Use researcher only for external/technical research tasks.
  • Do not fire every agent on every task. The orchestrator selects the minimum set and stops unnecessary chains.

docs.title: Orchestrator behavior
docs.text:
• Prefer "one strong planning call + one implementation agent + one QA/review loop" over spawning many redundant agents.
  • The orchestrator never implements directly.
  • The orchestrator detects design decisions and delegates those to the brainstormer instead of deciding alone.

docs.title: Collaborative brainstorming
docs.text:
• Runs as independent proposals -> cross-critique -> synthesis among only the relevant specialists (2-4), then selects a solution autonomously.
  • Durable report written to docs/ai/brainstorms/BR-NNN-<topic>.md; long-term decisions recorded as ADRs.
  • Agents are autonomous by default: analyze, discuss, decide, report, implement. The user receives the decision as a report and can override later.
  • Never stop simply because several solutions exist. Block only when the task is genuinely unsafe, impossible, or contradictory (BLOCKED report).

docs.title: Nesting note
docs.text: The standard workflow keeps subagent delegation to one level, but the brainstorming phase intentionally runs one extra level (orchestrator -> brainstormer -> specialists) as designed.

docs.title: Cheap/free model rules
docs.text:
The system is intentionally optimized for low-cost models.

  1. Give agents one task at a time.
  2. Keep prompts short and repository rules centralized in AGENTS.md.
  3. Load documents lazily.
  4. Prefer deterministic checklists.
  5. Use specialized read-only reviewers instead of asking one model to reason about everything.
  6. Limit subagent nesting to one level.
  7. Avoid repeated whole-repository scans.
  8. Ask the model to inspect relevant files first.
  9. Use automated tests as the main correctness feedback mechanism.
  10. Make the model produce structured output.
  11. Never rely on hidden conversation memory for critical architecture decisions.
  12. Put durable knowledge into the repository.

docs.title: Agent budget policy
docs.text:
For a small task:

Implementation only

For a normal feature:

Product-planner -> Architect -> Implementer -> Reviewer

For a high-risk feature:

Brainstorming (when a design decision exists)
  -> Product-planner -> Architect -> Implementer -> Reviewer -> QA

(Add security-reviewer when authentication/authorization, household data, financial logic, or external integrations are involved.)

Do not launch all agents for every trivial change.

docs.title: Fallback policy
docs.text: See docs/ai/model-strategy.md. Fallbacks are optional and depend on the configured providers. After two materially similar failures, escalate or change strategy instead of blindly retrying.

docs.title: Agent Workflow — reading the repository from GitHub
docs.text: This document explains how the SharedHousehold agent team operates and how a human owner runs the project from GitHub Issues and Pull Requests, with OpenCode executing behind the scenes in GitHub Actions.

docs.title: The pipeline at a glance
docs.text:
Human (GitHub)
   │  creates / edits / comments an Issue
   ▼
GitHub Event / orchestration workflow
   │  (opencode-command.yml, opencode-issue-triage.yml, opencode-pr-review.yml,
   │   opencode-agent-status.yml)
   ▼
OpenCode Orchestrator (primary agent, runs in a GitHub Actions runner)
   │  task tool → product-planner / brainstormer / architect / implementers /
   │              qa / reviewers / security / documentation / researcher
   ▼
Implementation → branch → commits → Pull Request
   ▼
QA → Code review (→ security review when relevant)
   ▼
Human approval (default gate) → merge → CI (ci.yml) → done

GitHub is the system of record. The repository is the system of knowledge (docs/, decisions, code). OpenCode is the execution engine and is deliberately transient — a new OpenCode process reconstructs state by reading GitHub and the repository.

docs.title: How an Issue moves through the system
1. Issue created → triage
docs.text:
opencode-issue-triage.yml runs on issues: opened. The orchestrator:

  1. reads the issue and relevant docs,
  2. decides whether a design decision is required,
  3. brainstorms if needed (writes docs/ai/brainstorms/BR-NNN-*.md, posts a concise summary on the Issue),
  4. marks the Issue status:ready (or status:discovery + open questions).

Implementation is never started automatically. It requires an explicit /oc implement from a trusted human.

docs.title: 2. Command
docs.text: A human comments /oc <command> (optionally /oc @agent <command>). The opencode-command.yml workflow validates the actor, assigns a run ID, posts a start/complete status on the Issue, and runs OpenCode.

docs.title: 3. Implementation
docs.text: /oc implement → the orchestrator selects the implementation agent, creates a branch (feature/EXP-105-* or agent/<topic>-<agent>), commits with Git trailers (Agent, Agent-Run, Issue), opens a PR, and posts the PR link. When needed, /oc plan runs first: it writes docs/ai/plans/PLAN-*.md on a plan/<issue>-* branch and opens a PR that /oc implement then executes. Human approval remains the default merge gate.

docs.title: 4. QA and review
docs.text:
• opencode-pr-review.yml runs a read-only review automatically for human-authored PRs (skips bot-authored PRs to prevent self-review).
  • opencode-pr-review.yml and /oc qa / /oc review run the QA and review agents, which post PASS/FAIL evidence on the PR/Issue.

docs.title: 5. Human approval
docs.text: The human reviews the PR in GitHub, asks for fixes via comments or /oc, and merges. CI (ci.yml, mvn verify) runs on every push/PR.

docs.title: Status (the issue state machine)
docs.text:
BACKLOG → DISCOVERY → READY → IN_PROGRESS → REVIEW → QA → DONE
                                ↘ BLOCKED
Label Meaning Applied when status:backlog created, not started created status:discovery analyzing/brainstorming/planning triage, /oc analyze, /oc brainstorm, /oc plan, /oc decide status:ready specified, implementation can start triage completes with a sufficient spec status:in-progress implementation running /oc implement status:review pending code review /oc review, automatic PR review status:qa waiting for QA verification /oc qa status:blocked waiting on a human or external dependency /oc stop, a BLOCKED report status:done complete and merged merged

docs.title: Type
docs.text: type:feature, type:bug, type:architecture, type:technical-debt, type:brainstorm.

docs.title: Priority
docs.text: priority:p0 (blocker) … priority:p3 (lowest).

docs.title: Agent (logical identity)
docs.text: agent:orchestrator, agent:product, agent:architect, agent:backend, agent:frontend, agent:qa, agent:security, agent:review, agent:documentation. These record which logical agent is/was active — there is one automation identity, not fake per-agent users.

docs.title: Status markers
docs.text:
Meaningful state changes are posted as standardized comments:

🤖 STARTED | 🤖 ANALYZING | 🤖 BRAINSTORMING | 🤖 PLANNING | 🤖 IMPLEMENTING
🤖 TESTING | 🤖 REVIEWING | 🤖 BLOCKED | 🤖 COMPLETED

These are concise; durable analysis lives in docs/ai/brainstorms/ and PRs.

docs.title: Run IDs and identity
docs.text:
Every execution has a run ID: run-YYYY-MM-DD-NNNN.

Where to find a run ID:

  • in the status comments on the Issue/PR,
  • in Git trailers on agent commits,
  • in the PR's AI Execution table,
  • in brainstorm/decision reports,
  • in workflow logs.

The run ID ties a human request → Issue → agent → model → branch → commits → PR → QA/review → merge. See the audit chain below.

docs.title: The audit chain (traceability)
docs.text:
For any task you should be able to answer:

Question Where to look Who requested it? the issue creator / command comment author (github.actor) Which Issue? Issue: #N trailers, Closes #N Which agent? Agent: <name> trailers/comments, agent:* labels Which run? Agent-Run: run-… trailers, status comments Which model? the AI Execution table on the PR + .github/oc-models.json Which decision? docs/ai/brainstorms/BR-NNN-*.md + ADRs Which files changed? the PR diff Which branch / commits? the PR Which tests? CI run + QA comment evidence Which reviewers? review comments + status:review Who approved/meged? the PR "merged by" info

Chain shape:

Human → Issue #N → Run ID → Brainstorm report → ADR → Branch → Commit(s)
      → PR → QA result → Security result → Human approval → Merge

docs.title: GitHub Project (fields)
docs.text:
A GitHub Project v2 can hold status automation. Recommended fields:

Status, Type, Priority, Domain, Agent, Current Run, Milestone, Risk, AI Decision.

Automating these fields requires a token that can write the Project (project scope for classic PAT, or a fine-grained token with "Projects" read/write) and org/owner setup — that is intentionally NOT embedded in the workflows or the repo (no credentials in the repository). Set it up manually and connect the Status field to the status:* labels if you want Board integration.

docs.title: Human overrides
docs.text:
An explicit human comment always overrides an earlier agent decision. Example:

Agent: I selected option B.
Human: /oc use option A instead

The orchestrator records the override, explains impact, updates the plan, and continues with option A.

docs.title: Loop protection
docs.text: Workflows ignore comments/issues authored by bot actors (*[bot]). Moving the state forward is always the human's action; agent comments cannot re-trigger themselves. PRs created by the agent team use GITHUB_TOKEN, so they do not spur new auto-review runs — review is requested explicitly or runs once for human-authored PRs.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: If a workflow fails, a model times out, or a partial implementation exists, recover by running opencode-agent-status from the Actions tab (or comment /oc status): the orchestrator inspects existing branches, PRs, comments, run metadata, and CI, then reports current state and the recommended next action instead of duplicating work.

docs.title: Required / recommended GitHub setup
docs.text:
• Labels: bash scripts/setup-labels.sh (upsert the standardized label set).
  • Repository variable OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS: CSV of human accounts allowed to run mutation commands, e.g. oussAbd.
  • Secrets (all optional): OPENCODE_API_KEY (OpenCode gateway/team key), provider keys (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) if models move off the free gateway.
  • GitHub Project v2 fields: see above (manual).
  • Branch protection on main (requires a paid plan; convention-only otherwise: agents never merge).

docs.title: Context management
docs.text: Use a layered context strategy. Agents must not dump the entire repository into context.

docs.title: Layer 1: Always available
docs.text:
AGENTS.md
current issue

docs.title: Layer 2: Load only when needed
docs.text:
domain-model.md
architecture.md
security.md
relevant ADRs
relevant source files

docs.title: Layer 3: Task-specific
docs.text:
specific module
specific tests
specific migration
specific API contract

For a feature change, the preferred order is:

Issue
 -> AGENTS.md
 -> relevant docs
 -> affected code
 -> tests
 -> implementation
 -> targeted verification

docs.title: Context-efficiency rules
docs.text:
• Never read the entire repository unless necessary.
  • Start with the issue and affected files.
  • Search before reading large files.
  • Read only relevant sections.
  • Prefer existing implementations/patterns.
  • Do not repeat information already present in repository documentation.
  • Do not include entire source files in prompts or reports.
  • Keep intermediate outputs concise.
  • Do not call multiple agents when one agent can solve the task.
  • Do not repeatedly retry the same failed approach.
  • Use targeted tests before the complete suite.
  • After two materially similar failures, escalate or change strategy.

These rules are also recorded in AGENTS.md and embedded in agent prompts.

docs.title: Brainstorming context strategy
docs.text:
For a brainstorming session, give each participant minimal independent context, never the whole repository:

Problem
+ relevant documentation
+ small set of relevant files
+ specific question

Do not send:

entire repository
+ entire architecture
+ all documentation
  • Independent proposals receive minimal context; only the synthesis step combines the relevant proposals.
  • Default: 2-4 specialist agents + one synthesis pass. For very simple design questions, 2 agents + synthesis is sufficient.
  • Limit discussion to 3 rounds (proposals, cross-critique, synthesis) maximum.

docs.title: GitHub Agent Commands
docs.text: The human owner drives the agent team from GitHub. Comment on an Issue or PR with a command starting with /oc (the /opencode alias also works). OpenCode runs inside GitHub Actions using the repository's configured agents and models.

docs.title: Command list
docs.text: Command Group What it does Changes code? /oc analyze <topic> analysis Reads the issue/thread and posts an analysis no /oc brainstorm <topic> planning Runs collaborative brainstorming, writes docs/ai/brainstorms/BR-NNN-*.md, posts a summary comment writes reports /oc plan <feature> planning Writes docs/ai/plans/PLAN-*.md, opens a plan PR no /oc implement implementation Verifies readiness, creates a branch, implements, tests, opens/updates a PR yes /oc review review Independent code review of the current change/PR no /oc qa [criteria] QA Verifies acceptance criteria with test evidence (PASS/FAIL/BLOCKED) no (tests only) /oc decide <options> decision Evaluates alternatives and records a decision writes decisions /oc continue control Resumes the last approved flow depends /oc stop control Halts current work, marks status:blocked no /oc explain <topic> read-only Explains an issue, a decision, or a design no /oc investigate <topic> read-only Investigates and reports findings no /oc status read-only Reports current state and recovery status no

docs.title: Targeting an agent
docs.text:
Prefix with @<agent> to direct the work to one logical agent. The orchestrator delegates to the named agent.

/oc @architect analyze the persistence options
/oc @qa verify the acceptance criteria
/oc @security review authorization
/oc @backend explain the Money rounding rule

Valid agent names:

orchestrator, brainstormer, product-planner, architect, backend-implementer, frontend-implementer, qa-engineer, code-reviewer, security-reviewer, documentation, researcher.

docs.title: Read-only vs. modifying commands
docs.text:
• Read-only (explain, investigate, status): run for any non-bot actor, with minimal permissions. Good for public discussions.
  • Modifying (analyze, brainstorm, plan, decide, implement, review, qa, continue, stop): only run for trusted actors* listed in the repository variable OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS. An untrusted request is rejected with a comment.

> analyze, review, qa can write reports/decisions or test artifacts, so they are treated as modifying for permission purposes.

Trigger phrases are case-insensitive (/OC, Oc are fine).

docs.title: Natural language is preserved
docs.text:
Everything after the command is kept. The agents read the full issue thread (description + all comments), so you do not need to restate the requirement.

/oc implement but use the simpler approach discussed by QA

The orchestrator receives the Issue, relevant comments, brainstorm report, decision, and your command. Your latest explicit instruction wins.

docs.title: Typical lifecycles
docs.text:
Feature:

1. Create the Issue (product description, acceptance criteria if you have them).
2. (optional) /oc analyze this issue
3. Wait for triage; the team brainstorms + posts a plan, marks status:ready.
4. /oc implement
5. OpenCode opens a PR; review it in the Files tab.
6. /oc qa, then /oc review (or reply to the auto-review)
7. Fix requests: "please address reviewer finding 2 in the PR", or /oc continue
8. Merge in the GitHub UI.

Reopen/recover:

/oc status            → what is happening? what should happen next?
/oc continue          → resume after a partial failure
/oc stop              → I want this paused right now

Decision override:

Human: /oc use option A instead

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
• Status comments (🤖 STARTED, 🤖 COMPLETED, phase markers) on the Issue.
  • Concise agent comments with identity (Agent:, Run:).
  • Links to durable reports (docs/ai/brainstorms/, ADRs) instead of huge transcripts.
  • Commits carrying Agent: / Agent-Run: / Issue: trailers.
  • PRs with a Summary, Closes #N, AI Execution table, and Review status.
  • CI checks running mvn verify.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Do not paste instructions meant to bypass the trust model; commands are validated against OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS, not comment text.
  • Comments are not terminal transcripts: keep the thread concise; agents link to reports instead of dumping logs.
  • If a command seems to have done nothing, check the Actions tab for the workflow run, or run /oc status.

docs.title: MCP strategy
docs.text:
No MCP servers are configured during bootstrap. Nothing here invents server names, credentials, or URLs. This document defines intent and permissions for when MCP servers are added.

Only add MCP servers when they materially reduce repetitive context or provide controlled capabilities. Keep MCP documentation separate from agent logic.

docs.title: GitHub MCP
docs.text:
Potential capabilities:

issues
pull requests
branches
repository metadata
checks/actions
comments

docs.title: Database MCP
docs.text:
Potential future capabilities:

read schema
inspect migrations
read-only queries in development

Never give an AI agent unrestricted production write access by default.

docs.title: Documentation/search MCP
docs.text:
Potential future capabilities:

framework documentation
internal engineering knowledge
architecture references

docs.title: Recommended permissions by agent
docs.text:
product-planner
  GitHub: read issues, read docs, comments
  Repository: read
  Database: none

architect
  GitHub: read issues/repository
  Database: schema read-only

orchestrator
  GitHub: read issues/PRs, comments where useful
  Repository: read
  Database: none

backend-implementer
  Repository: read/write
  GitHub: branch/PR operations
  CI: execute/read
  Production: none

frontend-implementer
  Repository: read/write
  GitHub: branch/PR operations
  CI: execute/read
  Production: none

qa-engineer
  Repository: read (run tests)
  GitHub: read PR/issues
  Database: read-only (development)
  Production: none

code-reviewer
  Repository: read
  GitHub: read PR/issues
  Production: none

security-reviewer
  Repository: read
  GitHub: read PR/issues
  Production: none

documentation
  Repository: read, write docs only
  GitHub: read issues/PRs, comments
  Production: none

researcher
  Repository: read
  Web: read/search
  Production: none

Principle: reviewers and planning agents are read-only; only implementation agents get write access; nobody except approved humans touches production.

docs.title: MCP security rules
docs.text:
• secrets stay outside repository files
  • least privilege
  • read-only by default
  • development environment before production
  • explicit permission for mutation tools
  • document every connected MCP

docs.title: Model strategy
docs.text: This repository uses explicit per-agent model assignments so that every role runs on a model suited to its workload. Roles are preserved even if a specific model identity is unavailable; unresolved models are documented here rather than silently replaced.

docs.title: Why the OpenRouter :free agents were remapped (2026-09-21, chore OPS-003)
docs.text:
During OPS-010 verification, subagent runs failed with a free-models-per-day rate-limit message ("add 10 credits to unlock 1000 free model requests per day"). The four agents that had been assigned OpenRouter :free models (backend-implementer, frontend-implementer, qa-engineer, code-reviewer) were remapped to the OpenCode gateway free tier (opencode/*-free, verified working anonymously — see OPS-002) to keep the roster consistent and avoid depending on mixed providers.

Honest caveat: this remap does NOT bypass the daily free-model cap. The free-models-per-day limit is enforced by the model gateway for free-tier requests across providers and was already exhausted during heavy sessions. If the daily cap blocks subagents again, options are: wait for the reset, add gateway credits (1000 free requests/day per the message), or use a paid OpenRouter low-cost model. The original OpenRouter assignments are recorded in the matrix above as the revert target if an OpenRouter subscription is added.

docs.title: Model resolution in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
GitHub workflows run the orchestrator as the primary agent and resolve the model passed to anomalyco/opencode/github@latest from .github/oc-models.json — the single source that mirrors the roster above. The workflows never override a per-agent model otherwise; targeted @agent work runs through the orchestrator's task tool with each subagent's own assigned model.

Runtime details:

  • Workflows use use_github_token: true (GITHUB_TOKEN mode), so no OpenCode GitHub App install is required and workflow permissions stay per-job (least privilege).
  • Model endpoints in the runner are intended to be the same opencode/*-free gateway verified in OPS-002. If the runner cannot reach the anonymous free tier, add the OPENCODE_API_KEY repository secret (OpenCode gateway/team key) or a provider secret such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and update .github/oc-models.json plus this strategy together.
  • The free-tier daily cap documented below applies in CI as well; heavy GitHub-triggered runs may need gateway credits or a paid low-cost fallback.

docs.title: Cost profile
docs.text:
• Primary models are all free-tier or free-gateway models. The system is built for cheap/free operation.
  • :free OpenRouter models may carry rate-limit and concurrency constraints; expect them to be less reliable during peak usage.
  • Fallbacks 1 and 2 below are low-cost; fallback 3 is a paid model and is used only when configured.

docs.title: Fallback policy
docs.text:
Fallbacks are optional and depend on the model provider the developer has configured. Never hard-code a paid provider credential or API key.

When the primary model fails (unavailable endpoint, rate limit, repeated tool failure, context limitations, repeated unsuccessful implementation attempts):

  1. deepseek low-cost model available through the configured provider (e.g. openrouter/~deepseek/deepseek-flash-latest).
  2. glm low-cost model available through the configured provider (e.g. openrouter/~z-ai/glm-flash-latest).
  3. gpt-5.6-luna / the OpenAI luna family (e.g. openrouter/~openai/gpt-luna-latest) only as a final low-cost/high-capability fallback when configured.

Note: the literal identifier gpt-5.6-luna may not resolve in every installation; the ~openai/gpt-luna-latest alias is the supported spelling on OpenRouter. Verify availability with opencode models before use.

After two materially similar failures, escalate or change strategy rather than blindly retrying the same approach.

docs.title: Rate-limit considerations
docs.text:
• Free-tier endpoints commonly enforce per-minute/per-day limits. For planning agents (orchestrator, product-planner, architect) prefer fewer, larger calls over many small ones.
  • Keep agent prompts compact (see docs/ai/context-management.md) to stay within context limits and reduce token burn.

docs.title: Privacy considerations
docs.text:
Free does not automatically mean private.

  • Free third-party model endpoints may have provider-specific logging, training, and data-use policies.
  • Do not send secrets, tokens, credentials, or more data than necessary to any model endpoint.
  • Treat household financial data sent to any external model as sensitive. Where possible, prefer providers the team has verified, and keep prompts free of PII and credentials.
  • This document contains no secrets, tokens, or credentials.

docs.title: Unresolved items / human configuration
docs.text:
• Verified (2026-09-21, chore OPS-002): the opencode/*-free identifiers (opencode/nemotron-3-ultra-free, opencode/nemotron-3.5-lightning-free, opencode/ling-3.0-flash-fin-free) are served by the OpenCode gateway and respond anonymously — no API key or billing required for the free-tier models. They were probed with a one-turn opencode run --model ... check.
  • Verify all identifiers resolve locally: opencode models
  • After any change to agent/model configuration, restart OpenCode so the new configuration is loaded.

docs.title: Brainstorming reports
docs.text:
This directory stores durable brainstorming decision reports.

Naming convention:

BR-001-<short-topic>.md
BR-002-<short-topic>.md
...

Use the next number after the highest existing report.

Every report:

  • references its GitHub Issue (Issue: #123)
  • follows the template in .opencode/skills/brainstorming/SKILL.md
  • is a decision artifact (concise), not a transcript of the agent discussion
  • records the selected solution, alternatives, trade-offs, risks, and confidence

Brainstorm reports are problem analysis. Long-term architectural decisions are recorded separately as ADRs in docs/architecture/decisions/.

No brainstorming reports exist yet; the first design discussion will create BR-001-<topic>.md.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text: Issue: #5 (https://github.com/share-org/share/issues/5) Date: 2026-09-21 Participants: security-reviewer, backend-implementer, qa-engineer, code-reviewer Status: DECIDED

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The OpenCode agent permission architecture has two critical inconsistencies identified in the baseline code review (issue #2):

  • C1: .opencode/agents/qa-engineer.md has unrestricted bash: allow — the most dangerous permission in the roster, inconsistent with every other agent (orchestrator, code-reviewer, security-reviewer use git *: allow, *: deny).
  • C2: .opencode/agents/backend-implementer.md and .opencode/agents/frontend-implementer.md have NO permission: block at all — the two write-capable implementation agents are the least constrained and least documented.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• 11 agents total: 1 primary (orchestrator) + 10 subagents
  • 8 agents already have proper restrictive permissions following a consistent pattern
  • 3 agents are problematic (qa-engineer, backend-implementer, frontend-implementer)
  • Repository is a modular monolith with mandatory household isolation (AGENTS.md)
  • Agents never merge production code automatically
  • AGENTS.md security rules: "Never give database write access to unknown/untrusted clients", "Household isolation is mandatory"

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Must follow least-privilege principle
  • Must be consistent across the roster (follow orchestrator/code-reviewer/security-reviewer pattern)
  • Must not break agent functionality (implementers need to write code, QA needs to run tests)
  • Fix must be minimal and follow existing patterns
  • Valid permission keys per config schema: read, edit, write, glob, grep, list, bash, task, external_directory, todowrite, question, webfetch, websearch, lsp, doom_loop, skill

docs.title: Requirements

docs.title: Option A: Security-Reviewer (Strict Path Scoping)
docs.text:
Description: Narrow path allowlists (src/main/java/**, src/test/java/** for backend; frontend/** for frontend); bash restricted to mvn */npm *; QA gets test-only bash (mvn test*, npm test*).

Advantages: Strongest security posture; minimal attack surface; consistent with review agents.

Disadvantages: Backend path too narrow (misses src/main/resources, config, new modules); QA bash too restrictive (blocks mvn clean, mvn dependency:tree).

Risks: Legitimate development workflows blocked; frequent permission updates needed.

docs.title: Option B: Backend-Implementer (Broad Permissive)
docs.text:
Description: edit: allow, write: allow for backend; file-type patterns for frontend; bash allowlist for build commands.

Advantages: Zero friction for legitimate work; simple.

Disadvantages: Violates least privilege — edit: allow/write: allow with no path restrictions allows modification of agent configs, security docs, frontend code, any file. Inconsistent with roster.

Risks: HIGH — contradicts AGENTS.md principle applied to agents; security regression.

docs.title: Option C: QA-Engineer (File-Type Patterns + Test-Focused)
docs.text:
Description: File-type patterns (**/*.java, **/pom.xml, **/*.yml) for backend; QA has zero write; test-scoped bash allowlist.

Advantages: QA write-zero is correct; file-type patterns handle new files; test-focused bash.

Disadvantages: **/*.yml too broad (allows CI/CD, docker-compose); file-type patterns miss non-standard extensions; no sensitive path denies.

Risks: Medium — accidental modification of infrastructure config.

docs.title: Option D: Code-Reviewer (Pattern Consistency + Defense-in-Depth) ← SELECTED BASE
docs.text:
Description: Exact orchestrator pattern (map + *: deny fallback) for all tools; src/** + pom.xml for backend with explicit denies for .opencode/**, docs/architecture/security.md; frontend/** for frontend with same sensitive denies; QA gets mvn */npm * bash; explicit denies for webfetch, websearch, task, skill, external_directory.

Advantages: Maximum consistency; defense-in-depth; explicit audit trail; follows established convention.

Disadvantages: Most verbose; sensitive path deny list maintenance.

Risks: Low — denies are additive safety; can extend allowlist if needed.

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Key disagreements recorded:

  1. Backend file scope: Security-Reviewer (narrow src/main/java/**) vs Backend-Implementer (broad edit: allow) vs Code-Reviewer (src/** with sensitive denies) vs QA-Engineer (file-type **/*.java). Resolution: src/** with sensitive denies balances practicality and safety.

  2. QA bash scope: Security-Reviewer/Code-Reviewer (mvn *, npm *) vs QA-Engineer (test-only mvn test*). Resolution: Broader mvn */npm * — QA needs clean, dependency:tree, etc.

  3. Tool exclusions: Only Code-Reviewer proposed explicit webfetch/websearch/task/skill denies. Resolution: Include explicit denies for clarity and audit.

  4. Sensitive path denies: Only Code-Reviewer proposed .opencode/** and docs/architecture/security.md denies. Resolution: Include for defense-in-depth.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text: Issue: #3 (feat EXP-105 : expense shares) Date: 2026-09-22 Participants: backend-implementer, architect, security-reviewer, domain-modeler Status: COMPLETED

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement expense sharing across household members with explicit separation of: who paid, who participated, who owes, allocation method, and how a debt was settled.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• MVP supports EQUAL and CUSTOM splits (roadmap includes PERCENTAGE and SHARES for Phase 2)
  • Domain model defines: Household, Member, Expense, Money, Allocation, Balance, Settlement
  • Money value object exists with BigDecimal, explicit currency, HALF_UP rounding to 2 decimal places
  • Household isolation is mandatory (security.md)
  • PostgreSQL is the transactional source of truth
  • Modular monolith architecture with domain/application/infrastructure separation

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Never use double/float for monetary values
  • Currency must be explicit
  • Rounding rules must be defined and tested
  • Household isolation: member must not access another household's data by changing identifier
  • Domain must not depend on Spring or database implementation details
  • Keep business logic out of controllers

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Expense belongs to exactly one household
  2. Payer must be a household member
  3. Participants must be household members
  4. Allocations cannot be negative
  5. Total allocation must equal expense total (with deterministic rounding policy)
  6. Split methods: EQUAL, PERCENTAGE, SHARES, CUSTOM
  7. Audit/history strategy for expense editing

docs.title: Unknowns / Assumptions
docs.text:
• Exact rounding policy for allocation remainder distribution
  • Whether allocations are stored as derived values or computed on read
  • API contract shape for creating expenses with different split methods
  • Database schema for expense, allocation, participant relationships
  • How to handle expense editing while preserving audit trail
  • Whether to implement all split methods now or phase them

docs.title: Option A: Backend Implementer (Implementation-First)
docs.text:
Description: Explicit persisted allocations for all split methods. Strategy pattern in ExpenseAllocationService with HALF_UP rounding, remainder to first N by memberId. Single API endpoint. Database: expense + expense_allocation tables.

Advantages: Clear separation, testable, extensible, supports audit, simple remainder handling

Disadvantages: More database rows, allocation service needs careful edge-case testing

Risks: Rounding edge cases with many participants; service becoming god object

docs.title: Option B: Architect (Architecture-First)
docs.text:
Description: Hybrid computed (EQUAL/PERCENTAGE) vs persisted (CUSTOM/SHARES) allocations. Largest remainder (Hamilton) rounding. Separate authorization service. Clean layer separation.

Advantages: Clean architecture, fair rounding, optimized storage, explicit authorization boundary

Disadvantages: Hybrid complexity, two code paths, largest remainder harder to implement

Risks: Inconsistency between computed/persisted; authorization gaps

docs.title: Option C: Security Reviewer (Isolation-First)
docs.text:
Description: Application-layer authorization + PostgreSQL RLS as defense-in-depth. Pure domain allocation functions. Event sourcing for audit trail from day one.

Advantages: Strong isolation, audit built-in, pure domain logic, RLS safety net

Disadvantages: RLS couples to PostgreSQL, event sourcing overkill for MVP, more infrastructure

Risks: RLS performance; event table growth; authorization bottleneck

docs.title: Option D: Domain Modeler (Domain-First)
docs.text:
Description: Invariants in Expense aggregate. SplitMethod enum with factories. Banker's rounding (HALF_EVEN). Payer receives remainder. Separate BalanceCalculator.

Advantages: Strong invariants, encapsulated logic, intuitive payer-remainder, clean separation

Disadvantages: Payer-remainder may seem unfair; HALF_EVEN inconsistent with Money; enum bloat

Risks: Enum bloat; remainder policy disputes; invariant validation performance

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Key disagreements and resolutions:

  1. Persisted vs computed allocations: All specialists except Architect favored uniform persisted allocations. Architect's hybrid approach was rejected due to double code paths, audit complexity, and inconsistency risk. Storage cost is negligible for household scale.

  2. Rounding method: Money class uses HALF_UP. Domain Modeler proposed HALF_EVEN (banker's rounding) but this creates inconsistency. Architect proposed largest remainder (mathematically fair but complex). Consensus: HALF_UP consistently, remainder to first N by deterministic memberId ordering.

  3. Payer-remainder vs first-N remainder: Domain Modeler argued payer should get remainder (intuitive). Others argued this is arbitrary and may confuse users. First-N by memberId is more explainable and testable.

  4. RLS and event sourcing: Security Reviewer advocated for both as defense-in-depth. Others rejected as over-engineering for MVP, coupling domain to PostgreSQL, and YAGNI. Application-layer authorization with AOP is sufficient.

  5. SplitMethod enum factories: Domain Modeler proposed factories on enum. Backend Implementer and Architect argued this bloats the enum; allocation logic belongs in domain service/factory.

  6. Authorization enforcement: Consensus on application-layer checks via HouseholdAuthorizationService + Spring AOP interceptor. Repository methods require householdId parameter. RLS deferred.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Selected solution: Uniform persisted allocations with HALF_UP rounding, remainder to first N by memberId, Expense factory encapsulating allocation creation, application-layer authorization with AOP, single API endpoint, deferred RLS/event sourcing.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
1. Persisted allocations uniformly - simplest, supports audit/editing, negligible storage cost
  2. HALF_UP rounding consistently - matches existing Money class, no dual rounding modes
  3. Deterministic remainder distribution - by memberId ordering is explainable and testable
  4. Expense factory encapsulates allocation creation - keeps invariants in aggregate, follows DDD
  5. Application-layer authorization with AOP - clean, testable, no PostgreSQL coupling
  6. Single API endpoint with discriminator - simpler routing, extensible
  7. Deferred event sourcing/RLS - YAGNI for MVP, can add later

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text: Decision Trade-off Persist all allocations Slightly more rows, but uniform code and audit support Remainder to first N by memberId Not "fairest" mathematically, but deterministic and explainable Single API endpoint Slightly more complex request validation, but simpler routing No RLS/event sourcing Relies on application correctness; mitigated by tests and AOP HALF_UP only Consistent with Money; no banker's rounding complexity

docs.title: Rejected Alternatives
docs.text:
1. Hybrid computed/persisted allocations - double code paths, audit complexity, inconsistency risk
  2. Largest remainder rounding - harder to explain, more complex implementation
  3. Payer receives remainder - arbitrary, may confuse users
  4. Banker's rounding (HALF_EVEN) - inconsistent with Money class
  5. RLS + Event Sourcing - over-engineering for MVP, couples domain to PostgreSQL
  6. SplitMethod enum factories - bloats enum, allocation logic belongs in domain service/factory

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
1. Rounding edge cases - Mitigation: comprehensive unit tests for all split methods
  2. Authorization gaps - Mitigation: AOP interceptor + repository contract + integration tests
  3. Allocation service complexity - Mitigation: strategy pattern with separate class per split method
  4. Expense editing audit - Mitigation: updated_by/updated_at for MVP; design for future event table

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
1. Should ExpenseAllocationService be in domain or application layer? (Currently domain)
  2. How to handle expense deletion? Soft delete (status) or hard delete? (Hard delete with FK cascade for MVP)
  3. Should participantIds be derivable from allocations? (Yes for EQUAL/PERCENTAGE/SHARES; explicit for CUSTOM)

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: HIGH - Strong alignment across specialists on core decisions. Clear precedent from existing Money class and domain model documentation. Well-understood problem space with bounded scope (MVP: EQUAL + CUSTOM).

docs.title: Modular monolith
docs.text:
The first version is a modular monolith, not microservices. One deployable application with clear module boundaries.

Why not microservices first:

  • The domain (household ledger) has strong consistency requirements; distributed transactions across services would add cost without benefit at this stage.
  • Small team and small product: a monolith has lower operational overhead, simpler local development, and fewer failure modes.
  • The modular boundaries still allow later extraction into services if a module genuinely needs independent scaling or ownership — but that decision must be justified and documented in an ADR.

Containerization/Kubernetes can be introduced later if deployment requirements justify it. Do not over-engineer the MVP.

docs.title: Hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)
docs.text:
• Domain: pure business logic, no Spring or database dependencies.
  • Application: use cases / application services orchestrate the domain through ports.
  • Infrastructure: adapters implement ports (persistence, HTTP) and wire in Spring and the database.

Rules:

  • Keep business logic out of controllers.
  • Use explicit request/response DTOs.
  • Never expose persistence entities directly as public API contracts.

docs.title: Initial domain invariants
docs.text:
Initial rules — subject to explicit refinement, never silently changed:

  1. An expense belongs to exactly one household.
  2. The payer must be a member of the household.
  3. Participants must be members of the same household.
  4. Allocations cannot be negative.
  5. Total allocation must equal the expense total, subject to a deterministic rounding policy.
  6. Currency must be explicit.
  7. Financial calculations must be deterministic.
  8. A member must not access another household's private financial data merely by changing an identifier in a request.
  9. Settlement is separate from the original expense.
  10. Editing an expense must preserve a clear audit/history strategy once that functionality is implemented.

docs.text: Detailed authentication provider decisions are intentionally deferred. This document records the security rules and review lenses now; concrete provider choices (identity provider, token strategy) are separate decisions to be made with a human when authentication baseline work begins.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• Who the user is. Scope: login/registration as a roadmap item (Phase 0).
  • Provider and token strategy are deferred decisions.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
• Who can do what inside a household.
  • Authorization is separate from authentication and must be handled explicitly.

docs.title: Household isolation
docs.text:
• Mandatory. A member must not access another household's expenses, members, balances, settlements, or products by changing an identifier in a request (IDOR).
  • Every household-scoped read/write must verify membership before acting.
  • Never trust household identifiers coming from clients without authorization checks.

docs.title: Input validation
docs.text:
• Validate all inputs at the boundary: unexpected shapes, invalid identifiers, impossible amounts.
  • Validation errors must be meaningful and must not leak internals.

docs.title: Secret handling
docs.text:
• Secrets must never be committed to the repository.
  • Credentials stay outside repository files and out of logs.

docs.title: Auditability
docs.text:
• Financial operations should be auditable.
  • Editing expenses must preserve an audit/history strategy once implemented.

docs.title: Abuse / rate-limit considerations
docs.text:
• Public endpoints (e.g. invitation acceptance, expense creation) should consider rate limits and abuse controls.
  • These are design considerations for baseline work, not implemented yet.

docs.title: Review lens (for the security-reviewer agent)
docs.text: Authentication, authorization, household/member isolation, IDOR/access-control issues, input validation, injection, secrets, sensitive data exposure, insecure deserialization, dependency vulnerabilities, API abuse, tenant isolation.

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text:
Browser (untrusted)
  -> REST API (authentication + authorization at the boundary)
  -> Domain/application layer (enforces invariants)
  -> PostgreSQL (transactional source of truth)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Baseline code review (issue #2) found two security findings in the OpenCode agent configuration: - C1: qa-engineer has unrestricted bash: allow — the most dangerous permission, inconsistent with all other agents. - C2: backend-implementer and frontend-implementer have NO permission: block at all — the two write-capable agents are least constrained.

This violates the least-privilege principle and the repository's security rules (AGENTS.md: "Never give database write access to unknown/untrusted clients", "Household isolation is mandatory").

Reference: Brainstorming report BR-001, GitHub Issue #5.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Apply restrictive, consistent permission blocks to all three agents following the established orchestrator/code-reviewer/security-reviewer pattern (map form with allowlist + "*": deny fallback).

docs.title: qa-engineer
docs.text:
• edit: deny, write: deny
  • read: allow, glob: allow, grep: allow, list: allow
  • bash: { "mvn *": allow, "npm *": allow, "*": deny }
  • Explicit denies: webfetch, websearch, task, skill, external_directory

docs.title: backend-implementer
docs.text:
• read: allow, glob: allow, grep: allow, list: allow
  • edit/write: { "src/**": allow, "pom.xml": allow, ".opencode/**": deny, "docs/architecture/security.md": deny, "*": deny }
  • bash: { "mvn *": allow, "*": deny }
  • Explicit denies: webfetch, websearch, task, skill, external_directory

docs.title: frontend-implementer
docs.text:
• read: allow, glob: allow, grep: allow, list: allow
  • edit/write: { "frontend/**": allow, ".opencode/**": deny, "docs/architecture/security.md": deny, "*": deny }
  • bash: { "npm *": allow, "npx *": allow, "*": deny }
  • Explicit denies: webfetch, websearch, task, skill, external_directory

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
1. Broad permissive (edit: allow, write: allow) — rejected: violates least privilege, inconsistent, security risk.
  2. Narrow path scoping (src/main/java/** only) — rejected: too restrictive, breaks legitimate work (resources, test fixtures).
  3. File-type patterns (**/*.java) — rejected: misses non-standard extensions; directory patterns more maintainable.
  4. Test-only bash for QA (mvn test*) — rejected: too restrictive; QA needs clean, dependency:tree, etc.
  5. Omitting explicit tool denies — rejected: implicit deny per schema, but explicit is clearer for audit.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive: - All agents now follow consistent least-privilege pattern - C1 and C2 findings resolved - Defense-in-depth via sensitive path denies (.opencode/**, docs/architecture/security.md) - Explicit audit trail for all tools

Negative: - More verbose permission blocks - Sensitive path deny list requires maintenance - Edge-case file paths (Docker, scripts) may need future allowlist extensions

docs.title: Addendum (2026-09-22, GitHub-native operation)
docs.text:
To let agents operate inside GitHub Actions runners (the GitHub-native workflow), the bash allowlists were extended with git/gh commands:

  • backend-implementer / frontend-implementer: added "git *": allow and "gh *": allow (needed to commit, branch, push, open/update PRs). Existing edit/write path scoping and sensitive-path denies are unchanged.
  • qa-engineer: added "git *": allow and "gh *": allow (diff/evidence reporting). QA remains edit: deny — it never modifies production files.
  • orchestrator: edit/write narrowed to docs/** + AGENTS.md (reports, decisions); bash allows git * and gh * for state reconstruction and recovery reporting; task: allow (delegation) retained; websearch/ webfetch set to ask.

This is a controlled broadening for GitHub-native execution. It does not relax the human gate: write-capable implementer access in CI additionally requires the trusted-actor rule (repository variable OC_TRUSTED_ACTORS) and per-workflow job permissions; QA and reviewers remain non-writers. The original restriction was relaxed explicitly so the change is auditable rather than silent.

docs.title: Revisit Triggers
docs.text:
• If backend-implementer legitimately needs to edit files outside src/** and pom.xml (e.g., Docker, CI scripts)
  • If QA needs non-Maven/npm commands (docker, psql for test DB)
  • If new tools are added to the permission schema that these agents might need
  • If the agent roster changes significantly (new agents added)

docs.title: Agent protocol
docs.text: AI agents have bounded roles. The roles below are realized by the agents defined in .opencode/agents/; this document defines the contract each role obeys. See docs/ai/agent-strategy.md for how the roles are sequenced and docs/ai/model-strategy.md for model assignments.

docs.title: Orchestrator
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • read the issue
  • decide whether a design decision exists
  • decide whether specification is needed
  • select the minimum required specialist agents
  • launch collaborative brainstorming when a design decision exists
  • pass only relevant context
  • stop unnecessary agent chains
  • summarize state after every major phase

Must not:

  • implement directly
  • edit or write files
  • invent requirements

docs.title: Brainstormer
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • orchestrate a structured discussion (problem framing, independent proposals, cross-critique, synthesis) among only the relevant specialists
  • select a solution autonomously per the decision policy
  • write a durable brainstorming report to docs/ai/brainstorms/
  • create or update an ADR when the decision has long-term consequences

Must not:

  • act as a single-answer agent
  • implement production code
  • modify anything outside docs/
  • stop and ask the user merely because several solutions exist

Blocking is allowed only for genuinely unsafe, impossible, or contradictory tasks, and always produces a BLOCKED report.

docs.title: Product/planning agent
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • inspect the issue
  • inspect relevant product docs
  • identify missing business rules
  • produce implementation-ready requirements
  • call out ambiguity explicitly

Must not:

  • write production code
  • redesign the product
  • invent requirements silently

docs.title: Architect
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • inspect the existing architecture
  • identify affected modules, domain changes, persistence changes, API changes, migrations, and testing strategy
  • produce a compact implementation plan

Must not:

  • edit files
  • rewrite unrelated parts of the application

docs.title: Implementation agent (backend / frontend)
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • implement an approved task
  • follow the architecture
  • write tests
  • update required documentation
  • run verification (focused first, broader when useful)

Must not:

  • change unrelated features
  • redesign the architecture without an ADR or explicit request
  • alter product scope silently
  • claim tests passed without running them

docs.title: QA agent
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • map acceptance criteria to tests/evidence
  • identify missing scenarios
  • inspect edge cases
  • run relevant tests
  • report PASS / FAIL / BLOCKED per criterion

Must not:

  • redefine acceptance criteria without stating the discrepancy
  • modify production code
  • claim PASS without evidence

docs.title: Code reviewer
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • inspect the diff
  • look for correctness problems
  • detect regressions
  • inspect architecture violations
  • identify missing tests
  • report findings by severity

Must not:

  • modify production code
  • rewrite the implementation

docs.title: Security reviewer
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • inspect security boundaries and tenant/household isolation
  • verify that a user cannot access another household's data by changing an identifier
  • check authentication, authorization, input validation, secrets, and abuse controls

Must not:

  • modify production code

docs.title: Documentation agent
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • update only the documentation needed by a task
  • prefer concise edits

Must not:

  • modify production code or configuration

docs.title: Researcher
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • perform external/technical research
  • return cited findings

Must not:

  • edit files
  • broaden the question into open-ended exploration

docs.title: Definition of Done
docs.text:
[ ] acceptance criteria verified
[ ] business rules covered by tests
[ ] implementation follows architecture
[ ] no unrelated changes
[ ] database migration included when required
[ ] API documentation updated when required
[ ] security implications reviewed
[ ] focused tests passed
[ ] broader tests passed when applicable
[ ] code review completed
[ ] issue linked to PR
[ ] documentation updated where necessary
[ ] ready for deployment/acceptance

Never claim a checklist item passed unless it was actually performed.

docs.title: Definition of Ready
docs.text:
An issue may enter READY only if:

[ ] user story exists
[ ] problem/context is clear
[ ] business rules are explicit
[ ] acceptance criteria are testable
[ ] edge cases are identified
[ ] non-goals are identified
[ ] technical constraints are known
[ ] dependencies are identified
[ ] expected test scope is known
[ ] task is small enough to implement safely

If the issue is ambiguous, it belongs in DISCOVERY.

An XL implementation task should normally be decomposed before entering READY.

docs.title: Publishing the documentation site
docs.text: Documentation and agent reports are rendered to a public GitHub Pages site, hosted in the dedicated public repository share-org/share-docs (https://share-org.github.io/share-docs/). The private share repository remains the single source of truth: editing docs/ there republishes the site.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The docs-publish workflow in share (.github/workflows/docs-publish.yml):

  1. Triggers on pushes to main touching docs/** or mkdocs.yml, and on manual workflow_dispatch.
  2. Builds the MkDocs Material site from docs/ (config: mkdocs.yml).
  3. Pushes the built site to the gh-pages branch of the public share-org/share-docs repository, which GitHub Pages serves.

The GitHub Pages site in share-docs is configured to deploy from the gh-pages branch (root). GitHub Pages on the free plan requires the target repository to be public, which is why share-docs is a public repo containing only rendered static content — source code stays private.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. Create a fine-grained personal access token scoped to the share-docs repository only:
  2. GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token.
  3. Repository access: Only select repositories → share-org/share-docs.
  4. Permissions: Contents → Read and write.
  5. Add it as a repository secret in share named SHARE_DOCS_TOKEN (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret).

Until the secret exists, the publish step is skipped with a warning and the site keeps its previous content.

docs.title: Triggering a republish
docs.text:
• Automatic: any change to docs/** or mkdocs.yml on main.
  • Manual: Actions → docs-publish → Run workflow.

docs.title: Privacy note
docs.text: Anything under docs/ becomes world-readable once published. Keep internal notes (secrets, personal data, credentials) out of docs/.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A household may want to divide an expense proportionally without manually calculating percentages.

docs.title: User story
docs.text: As a household member, I want to split an expense by shares, so that members can contribute proportionally.

docs.title: Example

Alice = 2 shares Bob = 1 share Charlie = 1 share

Total shares = 4

  • [ ] every participant has a positive number of shares
  • [ ] total allocation equals expense total
  • [ ] rounding is deterministic
  • [ ] invalid share counts are rejected

docs.title: Tests

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
IDEA
  -> DISCOVERY
  -> READY
  -> ARCHITECTURE PLAN
  -> IMPLEMENTATION
  -> AUTOMATED VERIFICATION
  -> AI REVIEW
  -> HUMAN REVIEW
  -> MERGE
  -> DEPLOY
  -> ACCEPTANCE
  -> DONE

The central principle:

A coding agent receives a bounded engineering contract, not an open-ended feature request.

Every implementation task defines:

WHO?
WHAT?
WHY?
BUSINESS RULES?
ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA?
EDGE CASES?
NON-GOALS?
TEST EXPECTATIONS?
TECHNICAL CONSTRAINTS?

An issue may enter READY only if it satisfies the docs/development/definition-of-ready.md checklist; otherwise it belongs in DISCOVERY. Completed work must satisfy docs/development/definition-of-done.md.

The ARCHITECTURE PLAN step includes collaborative brainstorming when the task involves a design decision. The orchestrator detects this and delegates to the brainstormer, which selects a solution autonomously and writes a report to docs/ai/brainstorms/ (and an ADR where justified). See docs/ai/agent-strategy.md.

docs.title: Branch rule
docs.text:
One issue should normally map to one branch.

fix/EXP-212-rounding-error
chore/OPS-010-ci-baseline

docs.title: Pull request rule
docs.text:
A PR should:

  • reference one primary issue (Closes #123)
  • stay focused (no unrelated changes)
  • include tests
  • include a migration if needed
  • explain externally observable behavior
  • identify AI-agent involvement
  • pass CI before merge

docs.title: Human gate
docs.text:
AI must not be the final approver of a sensitive change. At minimum, human review is required for:

  • authentication/authorization
  • financial calculation changes
  • database destructive migrations
  • external integrations
  • production deployment changes
  • security-sensitive configuration
  • large architecture changes

Implementation and review agents never merge production code automatically. Agent-generated changes must be auditable (AI involvement recorded in the PR).

docs.title: Relationship to the roadmap
docs.text: This MVP is Phase 0 through the expense/balance/settlement part of Phase 3 in docs/product/roadmap.md. Later roadmap phases are hypotheses, not commitments.

docs.title: Personas
docs.text: Personas describe real problems, not demographics. They shape priorities and acceptance criteria.

docs.title: Roommates
docs.text:
Problem: splitting rent, utilities, internet, and shared groceries every month, tracking who paid, and reconciling who owes whom. Manual tables drift and cause conflict when amounts are not equal or someone paid for more than their share.

What they need: a clear record of every shared expense, an explicit split, current balances, and a way to settle up without arguing about the past.

docs.title: Couples / families
docs.text:
Problem: combining household costs (food, household goods, subscriptions, children's expenses) while keeping contributions fair and transparent. One person often ends up as the de-facto accountant.

What they need: a shared ledger they both trust, simple custom splits, and an auditable history that reduces friction and "who owes what" conversations.

docs.title: Friends sharing temporary accommodation
docs.text:
Problem: short-lived sharing (holidays, temporary stays, project housing) where expenses are unequal, commitments are short, and nobody wants to set up heavy financial tooling.

What they need: fast setup, clear one-time splits, quick settlement, and low effort to leave the group cleanly when the arrangement ends.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: These personas are initial and deliberately small. New personas may be added as the product grows, but persona changes are product decisions, not engineering decisions.

docs.title: Product vision
docs.text: Make shared household finances transparent, fair, and easy to reconcile without requiring spreadsheets, manual calculations, or constant messages between household members.

docs.title: Core user problem
docs.text: People sharing a household (roommates, families, friends) split bills, buy shared goods, and track who owes whom. Today this is done in spreadsheets, chat messages, and mental arithmetic. Balances go stale, disputes arise over who paid what or how an amount was split, and settling debts is awkward.

docs.title: Target users
docs.text:
• Roommates sharing rent, utilities, and groceries
  • Couples and families managing shared household finances
  • Friends sharing temporary accommodation or joint trips

See docs/product/personas.md for details.

docs.title: Initial value proposition
docs.text: A transparent household ledger where every expense records who paid, who participated, how the amount was allocated, and how debts are settled. Any member can see the state and trust the numbers, because the rules are explicit and the calculations are deterministic.

docs.title: Long-term direction
docs.text:
The system is intentionally a household ledger and allocation system, not just an expense-splitting calculator. Future concepts (recurring expenses, shared products, shopping lists) build on the same core model.

Future phases documented in docs/product/roadmap.md are hypotheses, not commitments. They are pursued only when the current phase is stable and the need is real.

docs.title: Non-goals (for now)
docs.text: Bank integration, payment providers, OCR, AI assistants, cryptocurrency, taxes, multi-currency conversion, marketplaces, and microservices are all out of scope for the MVP. See docs/product/mvp.md.
